verses.text: One day as Jesus was teaching the people in the temple courts and proclaiming the gospel, the chief priests and scribes, together with the elders, came up to Him.
"Tell us," they said, "by what authority are You doing these things, and who gave You this authority?"
"I will also ask you a question," Jesus replied. "Tell Me:
John's baptism—was it from heaven, or from men?"
They deliberated among themselves and said, "If we say, 'From heaven,' He will ask, 'Why did you not believe him?'
But if we say, 'From men,' all the people will stone us, for they are convinced that John was a prophet."
So they answered that they did not know where it was from.
And Jesus replied, "Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things."
Then He proceeded to tell the people this parable: "A man planted a vineyard, rented it out to some tenants, and went away for a long time.
At harvest time, he sent a servant to the tenants to collect his share of the fruit of the vineyard. But the tenants beat the servant and sent him away empty-handed.
So he sent another servant, but they beat him and treated him shamefully, sending him away empty-handed.
Then he sent a third, but they wounded him and threw him out.
'What shall I do?' asked the owner of the vineyard. 'I will send my beloved son. Perhaps they will respect him.'
But when the tenants saw the son, they discussed it among themselves and said, 'This is the heir. Let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.'
So they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them?
He will come and kill those tenants and give the vineyard to others." And when the people heard this, they said, "May such a thing never happen!"
But Jesus looked directly at them and said, "Then what is the meaning of that which is written: 'The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone'?
Everyone who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces, but he on whom it falls will be crushed."
When the scribes and chief priests realized that Jesus had spoken this parable against them, they sought to arrest Him that very hour. But they were afraid of the people.
So they watched Him closely and sent spies who pretended to be sincere. They were hoping to catch Him in His words in order to hand Him over to the rule and authority of the governor.
"Teacher," they inquired, "we know that You speak and teach correctly. You show no partiality but teach the way of God in accordance with the truth.
Is it lawful for us to pay taxes to Caesar or not?"
But Jesus saw through their duplicity and said to them,
"Show Me a denarius. Whose image and inscription are on it?" "Caesar's," they answered.
So Jesus told them, "Give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's."
And they were unable to trap Him in His words before the people. And amazed at His answer, they fell silent.
Then some of the Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection, came to question Him.
"Teacher," they said, "Moses wrote for us that if a man's brother dies and leaves a wife but no children, the man is to marry his brother's widow and raise up offspring for him.
Now there were seven brothers. The first one married a wife but died childless.
Then the second
and the third married the widow, and in the same way all seven died, leaving no children.
And last of all, the woman died.
So then, in the resurrection, whose wife will she be? For all seven were married to her."
Jesus answered, "The sons of this age marry and are given in marriage.
But those who are considered worthy to share in the age to come and in the resurrection from the dead will neither marry nor be given in marriage.
In fact, they can no longer die, because they are like the angels. And since they are sons of the resurrection, they are sons of God.
Even Moses demonstrates that the dead are raised, in the passage about the burning bush. For he calls the Lord 'the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.'
He is not the God of the dead, but of the living, for to Him all are alive."
Some of the scribes answered, "Teacher, You have spoken well!"
And they did not dare to question Him any further.
Then Jesus declared, "How can it be said that the Christ is the Son of David?
For David himself says in the book of Psalms: 'The Lord said to my Lord, "Sit at My right hand
until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet."'
Thus David calls Him 'Lord.' So how can He be David's son?"
In the hearing of all the people, Jesus said to His disciples,
"Beware of the scribes. They like to walk around in long robes, and they love the greetings in the marketplaces, the chief seats in the synagogues, and the places of honor at banquets.
They defraud widows of their houses, and for a show make lengthy prayers. These men will receive greater condemnation."

context.author: Luke, the physician and companion of Paul
context.genre: Controversy narrative: a series of trap questions and parables in the temple courts during the final week
context.audience: The chief priests, scribes, and elders (v.1), the people listening (v.9), spies sent to trap Him (v.20), Sadducees (v.27), and the disciples (v.45).
context.setting: Jesus is teaching in the temple courts in Jerusalem during the week before His crucifixion. The courts were the busiest public space in the city and the natural place for rabbis to teach and debate. Each of the groups who question Him here represents a different part of the Jerusalem establishment: priests, scribes, elders, Herodians, and Sadducees.
context.custom: A denarius was a Roman silver coin worth a day's labor, stamped with the emperor's head and an inscription calling him son of a god, so many Jews found it offensive to carry. Asking "by what authority" was a formal challenge, as a teacher without recognized ordination was suspect. The Sadducees were an aristocratic priestly party who accepted only the five books of Moses as authoritative, which explains why Jesus answers them from Exodus 3.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 19 ended with Jesus cleansing the temple and teaching daily while the leaders looked for a way to kill Him. Chapter 20 is the leaders' counterattack: they challenge His authority, try to trap Him on taxes and the resurrection, and are silenced. Chapter 21 will bring the last public teaching and the discourse on the temple's fall.
context.timelineBible: Verse 17 quotes Psalm 118:22, the same psalm the crowd sang at the entry (19:38). The vineyard parable draws on Isaiah 5:1-7, where Israel is God's vineyard and the prophets are His servants. Verse 42 quotes Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse the New Testament quotes most often, to show that the Messiah is more than David's son.
context.sparkNotes: The chief priests, scribes, and elders ask Jesus by what authority He acts, and He answers with a question about John's baptism that they cannot answer without trapping themselves. He then tells the parable of the tenants, who beat the servants and kill the owner's son, and warns that the rejected stone has become the cornerstone. Spies ask whether to pay taxes to Caesar, and He answers, "Give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's." The Sadducees pose a puzzle about a woman with seven husbands, and He proves the resurrection from the burning bush. Finally, He asks how the Christ can be both David's son and David's Lord, and warns the disciples about scribes who devour widows' houses.

translation.meaning: The right or power to act, not just raw strength. The leaders want to know who licensed Jesus to teach and cleanse the temple, and Jesus answers by pointing to John, who came from God.
Literally "head of the corner," the stone that fixes the angle and alignment of a building. Quoting Psalm 118:22, Jesus says the Messiah is the rejected stone that becomes the cornerstone.
Craftiness, a willingness to do anything to win. Jesus sees through the sincere look of the spies and answers the real question under the pretended one.

A Hebrew way of saying those who belong to the resurrection age. Jesus says they will not marry or die, and are like the angels, not because they become angels but because they share in an immortal life.

commentary.note: Henry says the leaders' refusal to answer honestly about John means they lose the right to a direct answer: "Those that bury the knowledge they have are justly denied further knowledge." He reads the vineyard as the church's privileges, with God as landlord and the prophets as His messengers, and notes that "those who reject Christ's ministers would reject Christ himself." On the cornerstone, he calls Christ "the corner-stone and top-stone of the church," a stone over which some stumble and on which others are ground to powder.

On taxes, Henry says Jesus separates civil duty from religious duty: we owe Caesar civil obedience, but only God can claim the heart. On the resurrection, he warns that without this doctrine "all religion falls to the ground." On David's Lord, he says Christ is David's Lord as God and David's Son as man. Of the scribes, he writes that "dissembled piety is double iniquity."

Gill identifies the vineyard with the Jewish people and the servants with the prophets, and ties the vineyard being given "to others" to the Romans' judgment on Judea and the Gentiles' reception of the gospel. On the stone, he says those who fall on it by refusing Christ are broken, and on whomever it falls, "it will grind him to powder." On the Sadducees, he notes the saints will be "equal unto the angels," and he reads Psalm 110:1 as God the Father speaking to the risen and ascended Christ, who sits at His right hand.
